idiom_name: dynamic_cast<T*> cross-cast: null means the capability is absent
implementation_notes: The capability query is a sideways dynamic_cast to the interface class: `if (auto* r = dynamic_cast<Rollable*>(s)) r->roll();` tests support and yields the handle in one step. cppreference documents this crosscast case (the target must be an unambiguous public base of the most-derived object) and notes that the source must be polymorphic and that some forms rely on RTTI, which compilers can disable. What replaces the classic structure is this cast plus one interface class per capability; the classic form is still justified whenever RTTI is off or the value cannot be polymorphic, which is what the sibling variants cover.
pitfalls: Excessive capability queries mean the hierarchy is wrong (Dewhurst's Item 27; More C++ Idioms): if most call sites cross-cast, the operation belongs in the base interface.
dynamic_cast needs a polymorphic source type and RTTI; with -fno-rtti it will not compile, and the static_cast that often replaces it is undefined behaviour when the guess is wrong.
Cross-casts walk the class graph on every call, so query once and cache the handle on hot paths instead of re-asking per element.

variants.name: RTTI-free virtual query method (COM-style)
variants.implementation_notes: When RTTI is disabled, or the objects cannot share a common polymorphic base, invert the query: one polymorphic root declares a virtual query(const InterfaceId&) that every implementation answers by returning this cast to the requested capability base, or nullptr; a small function template restores type safety at the call site - `template <class I> I* query(Root* o, const InterfaceId& id) { return static_cast<I*>(o->query(id)); }`. This is the shape COM's IUnknown::QueryInterface takes with GUIDs as interface ids, and it is the portable choice for console, games and kernel-adjacent builds that ship with -fno-rtti. The price is that each implementer maintains the id table by hand.
variants.idiom_name: virtual void* query(InterfaceId) plus a typed function-template wrapper
pitfalls: Each implementation maintains its id table by hand: a forgotten branch answers 'no' for a capability the object really has, and the compiler cannot notice.
void* erases the type, so keep the cast inside the wrapper template (and beware that static_cast cannot verify the id really identifies that interface).
The id set and each id's identity must stay stable across releases, or callers that cached a negative answer keep believing it.

variants.name: std::any + any_cast for non-polymorphic values
variants.implementation_notes: For values that cannot be polymorphic (a parsed document, a plugin message, a functional payload), the C++17 realisation is a type-erased container: store the value in std::any and ask any_cast<T>(&a), which returns a pointer to the contained object when its type matches and null otherwise, so the shape of the query (handle or explicit negative) is unchanged and the 'interface' is the type T itself. The limitation is documented: std::any answers only about the contained type - it cannot ask whether a value implements a trait or satisfies a concept - and any_cast's value-returning forms throw std::bad_any_cast instead of returning a negative, so the pointer form is the one to use. Keep the id-based variant for -fno-rtti builds, since std::any needs RTTI.
pitfalls: any_cast matches the contained type itself (modulo cv-qualification), not a family: an any holding a Derived is not found by any_cast<Base>, and no other type relationship is considered.
The value-returning any_cast throws std::bad_any_cast on mismatch; only the pointer overload expresses an explicit negative, so always query with any_cast<T>(&a).
std::any may allocate for values larger than its small-object buffer and needs RTTI, so it is both slower and less portable than the id-based form.
